# Glossary

<!-- Generated by tools/state.py glossary from glossary.jsonl. Do not edit by hand. -->

**byzantine** (chapter 1). A fault model where failed servers may behave arbitrarily, including sending false or contradictory information.

**consensus** (chapter 1). The problem of getting a set of servers to agree on a single value, or a single sequence of values, despite failures and an unreliable network.

**crash-recovery** (chapter 1). A fault model where servers fail by stopping and may later restart, reloading their saved state and rejoining the system.

**disk write cache** (chapter 2). Volatile memory on the disk controller or drive itself that can buffer writes and lose them if power fails before the cache is flushed.

**durable state** (chapter 2). State stored on some medium that survives a process crash and reboot.

**fault model** (chapter 1). The explicit list of failures a protocol is designed to tolerate, and the failures it assumes never happen.

**fdatasync** (chapter 2). Like fsync, but forces only data and a subset of metadata, omitting metadata not required for later reads of the file contents.

**fencing** (chapter 1). Invalidating a stale leader's actions by attaching a number or timestamp to every decision and rejecting decisions that carry a stale one.

**FLP impossibility result** (chapter 1). The 1985 proof that in a fully asynchronous system, no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee that it terminates if even one server may crash.

**followers** (chapter 1). The servers in a cluster that accept the leader's decisions and replicate its state.

**fsync** (chapter 2). A system call that forces all modified data and metadata for a file out to the underlying storage device, establishing an ordering boundary.

**heartbeats** (chapter 1). Small periodic messages a leader sends to followers to signal that it is still alive and in charge.

**idempotent** (chapter 2). An operation that produces the same result no matter how many times it is applied, so replaying it is safe.

**leader** (chapter 1). The one server in a cluster that is currently in charge of deciding the order of operations.

**majority** (chapter 1). More than half of the servers in a cluster.

**mean time between failures** (chapter 1). The average time a machine or system runs before its next failure.

**page cache** (chapter 2). The kernel's in-memory cache of file contents; writes normally go here first and are flushed to disk later.

**partial synchrony** (chapter 1). A system model that assumes timing is not fully arbitrary, only that message delays and processing times eventually stay within some loose bound.

**partition** (chapter 1). A network failure that splits the servers into groups that can talk within the group but not across groups.

**persisted state** (chapter 2). Durable state that the protocol explicitly writes so it can be reloaded after a restart.

**quorum** (chapter 1). The minimum number of servers that must agree for a cluster decision to count.

**quorum intersection** (chapter 1). The property that any two majorities of a cluster must share at least one common server.

**replays** (chapter 2). The act of reading a log after a crash and reapplying its entries to rebuild state.

**replicated state machine** (chapter 1). A design where identical deterministic state machines on several servers process the same commands in the same order, so they compute identical copies of the same state.

**replication** (chapter 1). Keeping identical copies of some state on several machines so that the loss of one machine does not lose the state.

**split brain** (chapter 1). A failure state in which two servers in one cluster simultaneously believe they are the leader.

**stable storage** (chapter 2). Storage that survives crashes, typically a local disk with appropriate sync operations, though the Raft paper deliberately abstracts over the exact mechanism.

**volatile state** (chapter 2). State kept only in memory, such as the commit index and last applied index, which is lost when the process exits and reconstructed on restart.

**write-ahead log (WAL)** (chapter 2). An append-only sequence of records describing operations that must be applied to the state machine; the source of truth from which the state machine is rebuilt.
